hints: Look closely at tissue T in Fig. 5.1 at the bottom and left edge - it is pale-staining with many small trapped cells in spaces, and forms a thick supporting layer outside the muscle and epithelium.
walkthrough:
Recognise the Supporting Layer**
You can see T forms a thick, solid plate outside the airway wall. It contains scattered small nuclei in lacunae within a firm matrix. That appearance is typical of a strong supporting connective tissue.

Link Structure to Airway Function**
Bronchi need to stay open for air to flow freely but also be flexible. The tissue that gives this flexible support in the trachea and bronchi is cartilage.

hints: Think about what a ring of muscle around a tube can do when its cells shorten, and then relax again - what happens to the size of the space in the middle.
Connect that change in tube diameter to the volume of air that can reach the alveoli for gas exchange, for example during exercise or in dusty air.
walkthrough:
What Smooth Muscle Does**
Smooth muscle is involuntary contractile tissue. When it contracts it shortens and narrows the airway, and when it relaxes the airway widens again. We do not say the muscle does this on purpose to help breathing - it simply contracts and relaxes in response to nerve and hormonal signals.

Why Diameter Matters**
A narrower lumen increases resistance and reduces airflow, while a wider lumen allows more airflow. By adjusting bronchus diameter, smooth muscle helps regulate the flow of air into and away from the alveoli where gas exchange occurs.
Final answer: smooth muscle contracts and relaxes to change the diameter of the bronchus lumen, regulating airflow to the gas exchange surfaces.

hints: Start by recalling a single phospholipid - one hydrophilic head that faces water and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails that avoid water.
Now think how two layers of these molecules would arrange if water is present on both sides of the lamellar body membrane - where must the heads and tails point.
walkthrough:
Draw One Phospholipid Correctly**
Draw a small circle for the hydrophilic phosphate head and two wavy lines for the two hydrophobic fatty acid tails. That head-plus-two-tails symbol is essential for the first mark.

Build the Bilayer**
Place two layers tail-to-tail so heads face the aqueous fluid on the outside of the lamellar body and heads face the aqueous interior on the inside, with tails hidden in the middle. Label heads and tails if you can to make the arrangement clear.

Final answer: Drawing shows two rows of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads facing outward on both sides and hydrophobic tails facing inward; each phospholipid drawn with one head circle and two tails lines, arranged as a bilayer.

hints: Recall the normal role of cholesterol in a cell surface membrane - it sits between phospholipids and affects how fluid and flexible the membrane is.

Think about what must happen physically in Fig. 5.2 for release - the lamellar body membrane must contact and fuse with the cell surface membrane - how would a stiffer or less fluid membrane affect that.
walkthrough:
Cholesterol Controls Fluidity**
Cholesterol fits between phospholipids and keeps the membrane at the right fluidity - flexible enough to move and change shape but stable enough to hold together.

Fusion Needs a Fluid Membrane**
In exocytosis the lamellar body vesicle membrane must merge with the cell surface membrane to open a pore and release surfactant. If cholesterol is reduced, fluidity is altered and fusion is less efficient, so secretion of surfactant falls.

Final answer: cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity; with less cholesterol the cell surface membrane is less able to fuse with the lamellar body membrane during exocytosis, so less surfactant is secreted.

hints: Think about the normal job of a macrophage in the lungs and what would happen if old surfactant was left to pile up on the alveolar surface.
walkthrough:
Macrophages Clear and Recycle**
Macrophages engulf material by phagocytosis. Taking up old surfactant stops too much building up in the alveoli, which could block gas exchange, and allows the useful molecules to be broken down and recycled. They can also remove any microbes trapped in the surfactant layer.
Final answer: to prevent excess build-up of surfactant / to digest and recycle phospholipid, protein and cholesterol components / to remove pathogens trapped in surfactant.
